objection: Does ‘firstborn of creation’ mean Jesus was created?
answer:
Peace to you as well, and thank you for pressing this honestly—it deserves a careful answer, not a dismissal.

The key is that *prototokos* ("firstborn") in biblical usage is a title of rank and inheritance, not a claim about coming into existence. Psalm 89:27 calls David God's "firstborn," yet David was neither God's first nor only son in any literal biological sense—the word marks him as heir, preeminent, the one holding the place of highest honor. This usage was well established in Paul's own Jewish frame of reference before he ever wrote to the Colossians.

But we don't need to rest on comparative usage alone, because Paul immediately defines his own term. The very next verse, Colossians 1:16, says all things were created "by him" and "for him"—and then Colossians 1:17 adds that he is "before all things." If "firstborn of all creation" meant "the first created thing," Paul would be saying the Creator of all things created himself, which is incoherent. Instead, Paul places Christ on the Creator side of the ledger, receiving the same rank Genesis gives only to God: the one through whom, and for whom, "all things" exist.

This coheres with the wider witness of Scripture cited here: John 1:3 insists "without him was not any thing made that was made"—an absolute claim that excludes him from the category of "made things" altogether. Hebrews 1, quoting Psalm 45:6, has the Father himself address the Son directly as "God" whose "throne...is for ever and ever"—hardly language for a creature with a beginning.

So the "escape," as you put it, isn't a dodge of the text but attention to what Paul himself says the title means. "Firstborn" answers the question "who has supremacy and inheritance over all creation?"—and Paul's answer is: the One who made it all, and therefore stands outside the category of things that began.

transcript.content: Peace be upon you. I wish to press what seems to me a plain reading of your own Scripture: Paul writes that the Son is "the firstborn of all creation" (Colossians 1:15). In Arabic we say *awwal*, the first—and "firstborn" surely means He came into being before all else, does it not? If He were truly eternal and divine, why would Paul call Him *firstborn*? A firstborn implies a birth, a beginning. The Qur'an is clear: "He to whom there is no like" (Surah 42:11)—God alone has no beginning. So either Jesus had a beginning and is therefore created, not divine, or your own apostle's words are misleading. How do you escape this?
